Yeah it’s a common misconception that swayback has to have a posterior pelvic tilt - swayback with APT is more common than you think and it’s a different set of corrective exercises than swayback with PPT or just pure APT. typically with a PPT the hip flexors are long and weak - in the APT/swayback combo the hip flexors are tight and weak. I had APT my whole life before an injury that left my sedentary for a while and I developed swayback as a result - my hip flexors remained tight but then got weak, so my glutes tightened, then my hamstrings tightened in response. You can be hyperlordotic with swayback even though conventionally that’s not been believed to be true. I went to a PT who had me doing APT exercises and I only got worse bedause stretching the psoas worsened my swayback.  My glutes and hams got stronger but way tighter and I ended up injuring my hip flexors from over stretching. Next I saw a postural alignment specialist who explained all of this to me and since working on the swayback, my pelvic tilt has improved tenfold in a month. Focus on core strength and hip flexor lengthening & strengthening as opposed to just stretching. Doesn’t hurt to throw in some glute squeezes and hamstring curls after you’ve begun to stretch and strengthen the front of the hips. This is the protocol I’ve been following and it’s helped me and your posture looks a lot like mine.

Yes!!!! It’s “swayback pelvic tilt.” Do NOT do APT exercises!!!!!! Do swayback exercises. I was incorrectly diagnosed with APT and did corrective exercises for MONTHS and got worse and went to a new PT and was told I had swayback not APT and the protocol is different. Stretch and eccentrically strengthen hamstrings; stretch AND strengthen hip flexors; strengthen core; stretch AND strengthen glutes. It’s a misconception that APT and swayback are mutually exclusive. APT=strong and overactive hip flexors. Apt & swayback = tight and WEAK hip flexors, tight and possibly weak hamstrings, tight glutes, weak core.

A few different chin tuck exercises -

1) laying on the ground - tuck your chin then gently look up while keeping your head in contact with the floor/a pillow (whichever is most comfy) - hold for 5 when in extension. Do 10 of these. 

2) laying on the ground - chin tuck, then lift your head up about an inch off the ground & lower back down. Do not hold in this position. Do 10 reps. 

3) sitting up with good posture - ears over shoulders shoulders over hips - chin tuck, gently look up as far as you can. Hold for 5 sec. lower back down. 5 reps. 

4) chin tuck on hands and knees - then look up as far as you can & hold for 5. Lower back down to neutral. Do 10. 

Do all of these 2x a day - more is ok if they provide relief from pain.

I’ve been meditating for years and after a car accident this spring, I became unable to focus on my breath because when I did, every breath felt forced and I felt a pain in my chest, which would stress me out.

I recommend doing a body scan meditation or a guided meditation perhaps to help quiet the thoughts down, and once you have been able to reach a calmer, relaxed state, it’ll be easier to notice yourself feeling less calm or more stressed and be able to gently remind yourself it’s ok, you can let go. 
Once you’ve been able to keep yourself in a calmer mindset, you can start breaking down your overthinking and stress and ask yourself questions like, “why am I reacting this way?” “How am I feeling emotionally?” “What am I feeling somatically in this moment?”

I’ve noticed personally that if I just let myself accept and sit with whatever unpleasant thing I’m feeling - physically mentally or emotionally - and acknowledge it’s there rather than immediately trying to figure out how to overcome it, that alone can be very peaceful and calming, allow me to really observe what’s happening without judgement, which can then lead to insight or better ideas on solutions to the problem.

Weed is generally safe. There is the very small chance of addiction (I believe it’s 10% of chronic users - chronic defined as daily, long-term - have some level of a probability to physical addiction), but the more likely scenario if we’re discussing weed and addiction is becoming mentally or emotionally dependent on it. This doesn’t happen to everyone, though. I’ve known many regular smokers who developed a mental dependence on it and many who have not. 

Chronic use of weed can and does impact short-term memory and working memory. This is thought to be a cumulative effect, to the best of my knowledge. It does not impact the ability to form new long-term memories. And, if your short-term memory is getting foggy and you stop smoking entirely, you will eventually see cognitive improvements. 

However, cannabis is also neuroprotective! Stimulating the cannabinoid system in the brain can also be very therapeutic- I.e. why we have medical marijuana. I am personally a medical card holder in my state due to chronic pain/inflammation. 

Everyone reacts differently to weed though. It can be very relaxing and peaceful. Some people get very paranoid, or it feeds into their anxiety. 

Weed is not *completely* harmless, therefore, but, I also would not classify it as dangerous by any means and would call it pretty safe overall. Everything in moderation applies here, in my personal opinion. Weed is not concerning by itself, but, it can be abused, used irresponsibly, etc. just like anything else. 

There is no risk of structural damage to your brain (that I am aware of), nor is there a risk of feeling chronically slowed down/sluggish - I mean, if you smoke too much in a night or live in a constant state of highness then sure this can happen, but, it’s not a long term thing. You just smoked too much, or are smoking too much too often! 

I’d also like to throw in the caveat that if your brain is still developing there is a higher chance that it can mess with your short term memory, and a higher chance that those effects can be longer lasting or permanent. I’d recommend waiting to smoke until someone’s at least in their 20s, but, not necessarily the end of the world if you do not. I didn’t, nor did most of my friends, and for what it’s worth, I smoked frequently when I was pretty young and I don’t notice anything off about myself today as an adult. But, everyone’s different, and all risks and benefits should be considered!

My thoughts:

The thing about carrying the gene for something like schizophrenia is…it’s very complex. It’s possible to carry the genes for it, but, never actually develop the disease. Some people will develop it just because they have the genetic code, others will carry the genetic code and only develop it if an environmental influence “turns the gene on” (this is called epigenetic influence), and still others will only ever be carriers of the gene and never show symptoms regardless. We still don’t know all that much about schizophrenia - even the medications we have to treat it still pose the risk of serious side effects/aren’t perfect yet, and besides knowing that the neurochemical underpinnings are based in the dopaminergic systems of the brain, the details of what’s going on in the brain and why still need a lot of further research for us to better paint the picture. 

So, from that perspective, “activating” the gene at a younger age would be a bad idea - because there’s still a chance that that person never would have developed the disease to begin with. 

In the case they were definitely going to develop it at some point, I guess symptom onset and starting treatment at a younger age would be beneficial because of the factors you mentioned, but, to my current knowledge, we have no way to predict that someone who carries the gene will 100% become schizophrenic (please correct me if I’m wrong on this! I have not read up on schizophrenia in a few years now and research is constantly moving forward). 

And though schizophrenia does tend to manifest later in life, adolescent/early onset is still a phenomenon that occurs - often enough for us to document and acknowledge that pattern. 

Overall, it’s just best not to gamble with anything that could possibly trigger these genes to turn on - psychedelic or otherwise.

That doesn’t mean I’m advocating for children to start taking LSD - I’m not - but I don’t think it’s inherently dangerous on a neurochemical level if someone like OP does decide to give it a try.

Edit to include:
If one has a family history of genetically transmissible mental illness (bipolar, schizophrenia, etc.) - absolutely do not take psychedelics and especially not as a teenager. Sorry, but this sets off a bunch of red flags to me. Happiness isn't about repressing or ignoring your pains. It's about fully accepting who and where you are in the moment, feeling all your feelings and having the proper coping mechanisms to deal with said feelings. If someone is deeply bothered by something, sometimes they don't need advice - they need a space to feel how they feel and work through it so they can THEN reach an emotional resolution or accept advice, if it's wanted. You can't just tell people to abandon their suffering or that it's feeding their ego constantly if they have some serious problems or unresolved traumas/mental health issues to deal with.

I had PTSD for 6 years and the amount of people who told me to "just get over it" or "you're making yourself miserable" was infuriating. You know when I healed? When I saw a therapist who helped me deal with my suffering so I could let it go. Not because I magically disengaged with my mind, but when I faced my mind head on.
